page.pitfall: The most common pitfall: the receiver only accepts Base64 + URL-encoded data. Posting a raw JSON body is parsed as an empty data field — HTTP still returns 200, but the data is silently dropped.

http.name: HTTP / RESTful API
http.platform: Universal protocol · works with any language
http.summary: Every SDK ultimately speaks this protocol; languages without an SDK can integrate with it directly
http.step1Body: POST to the report endpoint with Content-Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded; the three form fields are the three protocol elements. GET works too, but the event payload would end up in the URL, so it is not recommended.
http.step1Code1:
curl -X POST '<endpoint>' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \
  --data-urlencode 'project=<project name>' \
  --data-urlencode 'token=<project token>' \
  --data-urlencode 'data=<base64(JSON array)>'
http.step1Note1: HTTP 200 only means the payload parsed; business validation and storage are asynchronous. Do not rely on the response body to tell whether the event was accepted.
http.step1Note2: The endpoint must keep the /receiver prefix (the gateway forwards on that prefix to the receiver).
http.step2Body: Each element of data is one event object. Field meanings: type (track for behaviour events / user_set for user properties / track_signup for login), event (event name, required for track), distinct_id (visitor ID, stable throughout), time (millisecond timestamp), identities (identity extension), properties (custom properties; a $ prefix marks a built-in property).
http.step3Body: Serialize the event array to a JSON string, Base64-encode it, then URL-encode the whole thing into the data field. Posting a raw JSON body is parsed as an empty data field: HTTP still returns 200, but the data is silently dropped.
http.step3Note1: A single event must be wrapped in an array as well ([{...}]).
http.step3Note2: The + / = characters in the Base64 result must be URL-encoded, otherwise form parsing breaks them.
http.step4Body: Before login, use a device or guest ID as distinct_id; after the user signs in, send one track_signup event with the login ID in identities.user_key and the previous anonymous ID in properties.$track_signup_original_id. Every later event then carries identities.user_key automatically, so the platform can merge the behaviour of one person before and after login.
http.step5Body: Put several events into one array and send them in a single request (10–50 per batch is a good size); one bad event does not affect the others. Retry a failed batch 3 times with a 500 ms × attempt backoff; when it keeps failing, queue the data locally and resend later so no event is lost.
http.step6Body: After reporting, open “Data management → Debug” and search by event name to see the latest reports (with property details and receive time); you can also pick the event in event analysis and check whether data appears. Latency of a few seconds is normal, and Flink-aggregated metrics lag by minutes.
http.faq1Q: The API returns 200, but nothing shows up in the platform?
http.faq1A: First confirm that data is the “Base64 + URL-encoded” content (a raw JSON body returns 200 with an empty data field), then check that project and token match and that the event name has no spaces or case mistakes.
http.faq2Q: Is time in seconds or milliseconds?
http.faq2A: Milliseconds (13 digits). Seconds (10 digits) are parsed as 1970; when omitted, the server receive time is used.
http.faq3Q: Can I post a single event as a JSON object?
http.faq3A: No. After decoding, data must be an array — write a single event as [{...}].
http.faq4Q: Is it safe to put the token in frontend code?
http.faq4A: Not recommended. A report token can write data; proxy reports through your own backend, or use a restricted report-only token.

php.name: PHP
php.summary: Report orders, payments, sign-ups and other events from your business code
php.step1Body: PHP 7.4 or later with the curl extension enabled (php -m | grep curl). No third-party dependencies.
php.step2Body: Three parameters: report endpoint, project name, project token. Read the token from an environment variable, never hard-code it.
php.step3Body: track() puts an event on the queue and sends it once the batch size is reached; time uses a millisecond timestamp.
php.step4Body: profileSet() writes user properties (overwrite); login() reports track_signup, merging the anonymous ID with the login ID so every later event carries identities.user_key.
php.step5Body: flush() serialises the queue to JSON, Base64-encodes it and submits it as a URL-encoded form; a failure is retried 3 times with a backoff. Call flush once before the process exits as a safety net.
php.step5Note1: http_build_query already URL-encodes the payload — do not urlencode it manually a second time.
php.step5Note2: For long-running processes (queue consumers, scheduled jobs) call flush explicitly at the end of each round so events do not sit in memory.
php.step6Body: After one report, search by event name under “Data management → Debug” — you should see the event and its properties, usually within seconds.
php.faq1A: Check that data is the Base64 value produced before http_build_query encoded it; make sure token and project belong to the same project.
php.faq3Q: Chinese characters turn into garbled text?
php.faq3A: Add JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE to json_encode and make sure the string is UTF-8.
php.faq4Q: Can I report synchronously inside a web request?
php.faq4A: Yes, but prefer a local queue (Redis or a database table) drained by a background job, so the request is not slowed down.

go.name: Go
go.summary: Report business events from high-concurrency backends with no third-party dependency
go.step1Body: Go 1.18 or later, standard library only (net/http, encoding/json, encoding/base64, net/url). There is no SDK module to import.
go.step2Title: 2. Define the event and the client
go.step2Body: The Event struct maps to the protocol fields; Identities carries the user_key identity extension.
go.step3Body: Track enqueues the event and flushes automatically once the batch size is reached; after login every event carries identities.user_key.
go.step4Body: Login reports track_signup to merge identities; ProfileSet overwrites user properties.
go.step5Body: Flush serialises the queue to JSON → Base64 → form encoding and sends it; a failure is retried 3 times with a 500 ms × attempt backoff.
go.step5Note1: When reporting concurrently, guard the queue with a sync.Mutex or give each goroutine its own client instance.
go.step5Note2: On graceful shutdown (signal → shutdown) call Flush once so the last batch is not lost.
go.step6Body: After one report, search by event name under “Data management → Debug”; you can also check in event analysis whether the event count grows.
go.faq1A: Check that data in the form is the Base64 string (Go's url.Values encodes it once more, which is correct) and that project/token match.
go.faq3Q: Does one invalid event in a batch affect the others?
go.faq3A: No. A batch is processed event by event; invalid events are skipped.
go.faq4Q: Do I need to handle the response body?
go.faq4A: No. HTTP 200 means the batch was accepted; only a non-200 response needs a retry.

unity.name: Unity (C#)
unity.platform: Client · Unity 2021+ / .NET Standard 2.1 (the same code also runs in a .NET console app)
unity.summary: Event tracking for games and C# clients: login, user properties, batched reports
unity.step1Body: Unity 2021 or later (.NET Standard 2.1, includes HttpClient). JSON serialization: Unity 6 ships System.Text.Json; earlier versions can use Newtonsoft.Json or install System.Text.Json through NuGetForUnity.
unity.step1Code1Label: Dependency note (pick one by Unity version)
unity.step1Code1:
// Unity 6 built-in: just using System.Text.Json;
// Older versions: install com.unity.nuget.newtonsoft-json from the Package Manager and switch to JsonConvert.SerializeObject
unity.step2Body: Three parameters: report endpoint, project name, project token. For client-side code let your own backend hand the token out (or proxy the reports through it) instead of hard-coding it into the build.
unity.step3Body: Track enqueues the event and sends it automatically once the batch size is reached; time uses a millisecond timestamp. After login events carry identities.user_key automatically.
unity.step4Body: Login reports track_signup to link the login ID with the anonymous ID; every later event carries user_key. ProfileSet overwrites user properties.
unity.step5Body: FlushAsync serialises the queue → Base64 → form encoding and POSTs it; a failure is retried 3 times with a backoff. In a game call it once when the scene changes, at settlement and before quitting.
unity.step5Note1: Never block the Unity main thread on the network: use async/await or start a Task from a coroutine so frames are not dropped.
unity.step5Note2: For reliability on flaky networks, persist the queue to a file under Application.persistentDataPath and resend it on the next launch.
unity.step6Body: Run one report in the editor or on a device, then search by event name under “Data management → Debug” to see the latest reports (with properties and receive time); confirm that events from the same player after login carry user_key.
unity.faq1Q: 200 returned but no data in the platform?
unity.faq1A: The most common causes are a missing Base64 step (raw JSON was sent) or a token/project mismatch; check the data field first, then look at the network.
unity.faq3Q: Unity reports that System.Text.Json is missing?
unity.faq3A: It ships with Unity 6; on earlier versions install com.unity.nuget.newtonsoft-json and switch serialization to JsonConvert.SerializeObject.
unity.faq4Q: Is it safe to ship the token in the client?
unity.faq4A: Not recommended. Proxy reports through your own backend, or use a restricted report-only token and rotate it regularly.

javascript.platform: Client · Browser H5 (modern browsers, zero dependencies)
javascript.summary: Web tracking: page-view and click collection plus a queue flush before unload; the 5-step event chain was verified end to end in a real browser.
javascript.note1: Pitfall: flushing on page unload requires `navigator.sendBeacon` or `fetch(..., {keepalive:true})`, and you must pass a `URLSearchParams` — a plain string is sent as text/plain, so the receiver cannot parse `data`.
javascript.faq1Q: Why are events lost when the page closes?
javascript.faq1A: Flush before unload with `navigator.sendBeacon(new URLSearchParams(form))`; handing a plain string to sendBeacon sends it as text/plain, so HTTP returns 200 but nothing is stored.

miniprogram.platform: Client · WeChat Mini Program (base library 2.x, zero dependencies)
miniprogram.summary: Tracking inside a mini program: `wx.request` reporting with a local cache queue and a `wx.onAppHide` flush; the language-level implementation is verified (on a real device you need to import it in the developer tool).
miniprogram.note1: Pitfall: `wx.getStorageSync` returns an empty string rather than null when the key is missing, so the storage adapter must normalise it — otherwise the anonymous ID becomes an empty string and the user cannot be merged.
miniprogram.faq1Q: Should request data be an object or a string in a mini program?
miniprogram.faq1A: Always pass a pre-encoded urlencoded string and set `header["content-type"]` explicitly: different base libraries serialise objects inconsistently, and a string is the safest choice.

reactNative.summary: React Native app tracking: global `fetch` reporting plus injected storage (AsyncStorage) and a flush when the app goes to the background; the transport and queue core is verified.
reactNative.note1: Pitfall: Hermes has no `btoa` / `Buffer` / `TextEncoder`, and `URLSearchParams.toString()` is unavailable in React Native too — implement base64 and urlencode in plain JS yourself.
reactNative.faq1Q: How do I do base64 and urlencode in React Native?
reactNative.faq1A: Do not rely on `btoa` or `Buffer` (Hermes has neither): implement base64 yourself and percent-encode segment by segment with `encodeURIComponent`, making sure `+` `/` `=` are all encoded.

android.platform: Client · Native Android (Java / Kotlin, HTTP transport)
android.summary: The Android tracking client core: device ID persistence, sessions, batching, backoff retries and a flush when the app goes to the background; the 5-step event chain was verified on the JVM (Java 8), but the APK has not been packaged and verified.
android.note1: Pitfall: `Base64.getMimeEncoder()` wraps lines at 76 characters, so you must use `getEncoder()`; `java.util.Base64` requires API 26+, and older versions must switch to `android.util.Base64`.
android.faq1Q: What transport should I use in production on Android?
android.faq1A: Just replace the form submission with OkHttp (`RequestBody.create(form, MediaType.parse("application/x-www-form-urlencoded"))`); the encoding and identity-field logic is completely unchanged, and the Kotlin call looks the same.

ios.summary: The iOS tracking client core: anonymous ID in UserDefaults, batching, backoff retries and a flush when the app enters the background; the 5-step event chain was verified with the same Foundation URLSession iOS uses, but the app has not been packaged and verified.
ios.note1: Pitfall: `addingPercentEncoding(withAllowedCharacters: .urlQueryAllowed)` does not encode `+` `&` `=`, so a `+` in the base64 is decoded as a space on the server and corrupts the data — encode the UTF-8 bytes yourself per RFC3986.
ios.faq1Q: How do I integrate this into an iOS app?
ios.faq1A: Add the client class to your project and call flush from `applicationDidEnterBackground` to resend; note that `URLSessionConfiguration` is copied when the session is created, so changing the timeout means rebuilding the session.

cocos2dX.platform: Client · C++ (Cocos2d-x; the engine side has not been packaged and verified)
cocos2dX.summary: The C++ reporting core (JSON / single-line base64 / form POST / queue) has been verified inside the engine; to integrate, just swap the transport layer for the engine's built-in HttpRequest.
cocos2dX.note1: Pitfall: swapping libcurl for `cocos2d::network::HttpRequest` (async + callbacks) is all it takes, but you must still keep base64 single-line and make urlencode encode every character yourself.
cocos2dX.faq1Q: Why not use libcurl directly in the engine?
cocos2dX.faq1A: You can, but it is not recommended: the engine's built-in HttpRequest reuses the platform network stack and handles callbacks on the main thread; the protocol, encoding, batching and identity fields are exactly the same as in the snippets on this page.

java.summary: Report orders, payments, sign-ups and other events from your business service; JDK 8 uses HttpURLConnection, and JDK 11+ can switch to java.net.http.
java.note1: Pitfall: `Base64.getMimeEncoder()` inserts line breaks, so you must use `getEncoder()`; base64 placed in a form still has to be urlencoded, otherwise the `+` is decoded as a space.
java.faq1Q: Can I switch to HttpClient on JDK 11+?
java.faq1A: Yes: replace the submission with `HttpClient.newHttpClient().send(...)`, use `BodyPublishers.ofString(form)` for the body and set Content-Type explicitly; the encoding and identity logic stay the same.

python.summary: Report business events from a backend service or script; `urllib` + `json` + `base64` is all you need, with no third-party dependency.
python.note1: Pitfall: `data` must be `urlencode`d and then sent as the body (you cannot hand the dict straight to urlopen); rebuild the Request object when retrying.
python.faq1Q: Will Chinese characters in property values be garbled?
python.faq1A: Use `json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")` and then base64; Chinese characters pass through unchanged, so do not transcode them again.

nodejs.summary: Report business events from a Node backend; use the built-in `fetch` + `URLSearchParams`, with no need for dependencies such as axios / undici.
nodejs.note1: Pitfall: give fetch a `URLSearchParams` instance as the body (it sets the urlencoded Content-Type automatically); a plain object is serialised to JSON.
nodejs.faq1Q: How do I control the timeout?
nodejs.faq1A: `fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(10000) })`; retry failures with a 0.5s / 1s / 2s backoff, and clear the local queue only on HTTP 200.

csharp.summary: Report business events from a C# backend; `HttpClient` + `FormUrlEncodedContent`, sharing the same protocol definition as the Unity client.
csharp.note1: Pitfall: when a repository holds both the Unity client and a server-side sample, an SDK-style project's default glob compiles the subdirectory sources into both projects (CS8802 / CS0579); exclude them with `Directory.Build.targets` (a `.props` file is overridden by the default Include).
csharp.faq1Q: How do I handle `$` inside strings?
csharp.faq1A: C#'s `$"..."` is an interpolated string: when building JSON, put field names such as `$SignUp` and `$track_signup_original_id` in ordinary strings, or escape them explicitly as `\$`, otherwise they are parsed as variables.

ruby.summary: Report business events from a Ruby backend; `net/http` + `json` + `base64`, with no gem dependencies.
ruby.note1: Pitfall: `Base64.encode64` inserts a line break every 60 characters (use `strict_encode64` instead); `$SignUp` inside a double-quoted string is interpolated as a global variable and becomes an empty string, so use single quotes.
ruby.faq1Q: Why does the event name arrive empty?
ruby.faq1A: Ruby double quotes interpolate global variables starting with `$`, so `"$SignUp"` yields an empty string. Write the event name and `$track_signup_original_id` in single quotes or escape them as `\$`.

c.summary: Report business events from a C / C++ service: hand-built JSON + your own single-line base64 + a libcurl form POST.
c.note1: Pitfall: libcurl requires a write callback (setting only `CURLOPT_WRITEDATA` makes it treat the value as a FILE*); implement base64 yourself and keep it single-line, percent-encoding `+` `/` `=` in full.
c.faq1Q: curl.h is not found at compile time?
c.faq1A: On macOS the curl headers live in the SDK: `-I$(xcrun --show-sdk-path)/usr/include -L…/usr/lib -lcurl`; on Linux just install `libcurl4-openssl-dev`.

lua.summary: Report business events from Lua scripts and OpenResty; with OpenResty you only need to swap the transport layer for resty.http, and the protocol logic stays the same.
lua.note1: Pitfall: luasec does not verify certificates by default — set `verify="peer"` explicitly and provide a `cafile`; it only accepts protocol names with underscores (`tlsv1_2`), and writing `tlsv12` fails immediately with invalid protocol.
lua.faq1Q: Lua has no os.setenv, so how do I supply configuration?
lua.faq1A: Read the configuration into an in-memory table and read values from there, or have the outer layer export environment variables; in OpenResty pass configuration through `ngx.var` or `lua_shared_dict`.

flutter.summary: Flutter app tracking: the web build was compiled and clicked through in a real browser with events verified in ClickHouse; iOS / Android were not packaged (no SDK available here).
flutter.note1: Pitfall: neither built-in Dart encoder works — `Uri.encodeFull` keeps `+` `/` `=` as-is, and `Uri.encodeQueryComponent` encodes space as `+` (collides with base64 `+`). Encode per RFC3986 yourself and assert the `data` field has no raw `+` / `=` before sending.
flutter.faq1Q: How do I know the Flutter web build is the new one?
flutter.faq1A: dart2js escapes non-ASCII literals as `\uXXXX`, so grepping for Chinese always returns 0 hits (easy to misread as a stale build). Search the escaped form instead, or compare `main.dart.js` size and build time.

batchImport.summary: Backfill historical logs / CSV into events (orders, payments, sign-ups already stored elsewhere): dry run, rate limit and resumable progress. Verified with 120 rows — 120 rows landed, resume re-sent nothing and lost nothing.
batchImport.step1Body: Shape a CSV by the column rules below (or a JSONL file with one event object per line). Keep `time` in the original millisecond timestamp so the historical moment is preserved; add `user_key` for logged-in events and `original_id` to bind the anonymous id.
batchImport.step2Body: `--dry-run` only reads, normalises, encodes and checks sizes — it sends nothing and writes no progress file. Use it to confirm the column mapping and see which rows are skipped and why.
batchImport.step3Title: 3. Send a small batch for real
batchImport.step3Body: Drop `--dry-run` to actually report. Start with `--limit` to confirm the pipeline, then use `--rate` to protect the receiver. The tool prints a run id (`backfill-<time>`) and writes it into every event as `properties.backfill_run_id` so you can verify by run.
batchImport.step4Body: Progress lives in `<input>.backfill-progress.json`; add `--resume` to continue after an interruption — completed batches are not re-sent. Failed rows are written with their line numbers to `<input>.failed.jsonl` so you can fix and re-run just those.
batchImport.note1: Important: the tool does **not** de-duplicate — replaying the same history file in full lands the same events twice. Always continue with `--resume`, or validate with `--dry-run` / `--limit` first. If the input file changed (content or mtime), `--resume` refuses unless you pass `--force-resume`.
batchImport.step5Body: Group the landed rows by run id (row count and event distribution) and reconcile with how many rows the file sent. The pipeline has a 1–3 minute delay, so re-run the query if needed.
batchImport.faq1Q: Do backfilled events keep their original time?
batchImport.faq1A: Yes: the tool passes `time` through unchanged (milliseconds) and the analytics side aggregates by event time. Do **not** replace historical times with the current time, or the whole history collapses onto the backfill day.
batchImport.faq2Q: What about a very large file (hundreds of thousands of rows)?
batchImport.faq2A: Run it in chunks: `--limit` for the batch size, `--rate` to throttle, and `--resume` to continue. The 50-events / 1 MB per-request limit is split automatically, so you never hand-split the file.

guideCommon.step1Body: Make sure the integration parameters are ready (see the top of this page): report endpoint, project name, project token. The protocol is always a form POST, and the `data` field = base64(JSON array) then urlencode — posting raw JSON returns 200 but the data is dropped.
guideCommon.step2Body: Use the command below to set up the runtime environment for this language; implementations that use only the standard library can skip installing dependencies.
guideCommon.step3Body: A minimal working reporting implementation for this language: event JSON → base64 + urlencode form → POST. The event time must be a millisecond timestamp; after login `distinct_id` always stays the anonymous ID, and the login ID goes in `identities.user_key`.
guideCommon.step4Body: After a successful login, send one `track_signup` event (`properties.$track_signup_original_id` = the anonymous ID) to bind the identity, and use `user_set` for user properties; every later event then carries `identities.user_key`, so the analytics side merges them into the same user.
guideCommon.step5Title: 5. Verify that the data is stored
guideCommon.step5Body: After firing the events, query `clklog.log_analysis` and check the 5 rows: anonymous track / track_signup / user_set / two tracks after login. The data pipeline has a 1–3 minute delay; HTTP 200 only means the payload parsed, so you must check the database to confirm.
guideCommon.faq1Q: Why does reporting return HTTP 200 but the database has no data?
guideCommon.faq1A: `data` must be a form field holding base64(JSON array) and then urlencoded. Posting raw JSON, a base64 value that contains line breaks, or a `+` that was not percent-encoded all return 200 while the data is silently dropped.
guideCommon.faq2Q: Event times are wrong, or one user is split into two before and after login?
guideCommon.faq2A: The time must be a millisecond timestamp (seconds are read as 1970); put the login ID in the top-level `identities.user_key` (not login_id), the anonymous ID to bind in `properties.$track_signup_original_id` (not original_id), and keep `distinct_id` unchanged after login.
